l: the LORD your God, Deuteronomy, Chapter 9
s: The LORD goes before Israel as a devouring fire to destroy and bring down the nations, driving them out because of their wickedness and to establish his oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He was angered by Israel's calf-making and wished to destroy them and make a greater nation of Moses, but listened to Moses' prayer.

Moses speaks to Israel, warning against claiming righteousness and recounting how he stayed forty days and nights on the mountain without bread or water to receive the tablets. He broke the tablets, burned and ground the calf, fell down before the LORD another forty days and nights, and prayed for Israel and for Aaron, appealing to the LORD's promise to the patriarchs and his reputation before Egypt.

Israel is about to cross the Jordan to possess the land, but is told repeatedly that it is a stiff-necked people who have been rebellious since leaving Egypt. They provoked the LORD at Horeb, Taberah, Massah, Kibroth Hattaavah, and Kadesh Barnea, and were spared from destruction only through Moses' intercession.

l: nations of the land, Deuteronomy, Chapter 9
s: They are described as nations greater and mightier than Israel, with great cities fortified up to the sky, and a great and tall people, the sons of the Anakim. The LORD will destroy them and drive them out before Israel because of their wickedness.

The land is called good and is to be possessed by Israel after crossing the Jordan. It is given not for Israel's righteousness but because of the nations' wickedness and the LORD's oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Moses also cites the land in his prayer, fearing others would say the LORD could not bring Israel into it.

l: stone tablets of the covenant, Deuteronomy, Chapter 9
s: The LORD gave Moses two stone tablets written with God's finger, bearing all the words he had spoken from the fire on the day of the assembly, after forty days and nights. Moses threw them from his hands and broke them before the people's eyes when he saw the calf.

The people made a molten calf shortly after turning from the way the LORD commanded. Moses took it, burned it with fire, crushed and ground it as fine as dust, and threw the dust into the brook descending from the mountain.

l: Israel's rebellion and the golden calf sin, Deuteronomy, Chapter 9
s: Israel's rebellion is traced from leaving Egypt onward, with the calf at Horeb as its central instance, provoking the LORD's anger to the point of threatened destruction. Further provocations are named at Taberah, Massah, Kibroth Hattaavah, and Kadesh Barnea, where they did not believe or obey the LORD. The LORD was also angry enough to destroy Aaron, for whom Moses prayed.

Moses insists that Israel's righteousness and the uprightness of its heart are not the reason it possesses the land, and warns them not to say so in their hearts. He states they are a stiff-necked people, and the reasons for the gift are the nations' wickedness and the LORD's oath to the patriarchs.

In Deuteronomy 10, Moses recounts how the LORD told him to cut two new stone tablets like the first and make an ark of wood. He went up the mountain, the LORD rewrote the ten commandments on the tablets, and Moses placed them in the ark he had made of acacia wood. A parenthetical aside notes Israel's journeys, Aaron's death at Moserah with Eleazar succeeding him as priest, and the LORD's setting apart of the tribe of Levi to carry the ark and minister, with the LORD as their inheritance. Moses says he stayed forty days and nights on the mountain, the LORD listened and would not destroy the people, and told him to lead them to possess the promised land. Moses then asks what the LORD requires of Israel: fear, obedience, love, and wholehearted service, grounded in the LORD's ownership of heaven and earth, his choice of Israel's fathers, his justice and love for the foreigner, and the growth of Israel from seventy persons to a multitude.

l: the LORD your God, Deuteronomy, Chapter 10
s: The LORD commanded Moses to cut new tablets and make an ark, rewrote the ten commandments on the tablets, and gave them to Moses. He set apart the tribe of Levi, listened to Moses, chose not to destroy the people, and ordered Moses to lead them to possess the land sworn to their fathers. He is described as God of gods and Lord of lords, great, mighty and awesome, impartial and unbribable, who executes justice for the fatherless and widow and loves the foreigner.

Moses, speaking in the first person, cut two stone tablets like the first, made an ark of acacia wood, and went up the mountain with the tablets. He stayed forty days and nights, came down, and put the tablets in the ark, then was told to lead the people toward the land. He then exhorts Israel about what the LORD requires of them.

Israel traveled from Beeroth Bene Jaakan to Moserah and on to Gudgodah and Jotbathah, and was spared destruction by the LORD. They are told to go in and possess the land sworn to their fathers, and are reminded that the LORD chose them above all peoples. They are commanded to circumcise their hearts, stop being stiff-necked, love the foreigner, and are noted to have grown from seventy persons to a multitude like the stars of the sky.

l: stone tablets of the covenant, Deuteronomy, Chapter 10
s: The LORD told Moses to cut two stone tablets like the first, which Moses had broken, and he did so and carried them up the mountain. The LORD wrote on them the same words as the first tablets. Moses then put them in the ark, where they remain.

l: ark (Moses' ark of acacia wood), Deuteronomy, Chapter 10
s: Moses made the ark of acacia wood at the LORD's command to hold the new tablets. After coming down the mountain he put the tablets in it, and they remain there as the LORD commanded. The tribe of Levi was set apart to bear it, and it is called the ark of the LORD's covenant.

The LORD wrote the ten commandments on the new tablets, according to the first writing. They are the words the LORD spoke to Israel from the middle of the fire on the mountain on the day of the assembly, and the LORD gave them to Moses.

At that time the LORD set apart the tribe of Levi to bear the ark of the LORD's covenant, stand before him to minister, and bless in his name, as continues to this day. Because of this Levi has no portion or inheritance with its brothers, since the LORD himself is its inheritance. Eleazar, son of Aaron, ministered as priest after Aaron died at Moserah.

l: Israel's requirements of devotion, Deuteronomy, Chapter 10
s: Moses states that the LORD requires Israel to fear him, walk in all his ways, love him, and serve him with all their heart and soul. They must keep his commandments and statutes for their own good, circumcise their heart, no longer be stiff-necked, cling to him, and swear by his name. They are also to love the foreigner, remembering they were foreigners in Egypt.

The speaker urges the Israelites to love the LORD their God and keep all his commandments, reminding them that they themselves saw his works against Pharaoh and Egypt, the Red Sea, the wilderness years, and the judgment on Dathan and Abiram. He contrasts the land they are about to possess, a land of hills and valleys watered by rain and under the LORD's constant care, with Egypt's irrigated gardens. Obedience will bring rain, produce, and victory over greater nations, with borders reaching from the wilderness and Lebanon to the Euphrates and the western sea, while turning to other gods will bring drought and quick perishing from the land. The Israelites are told to lay up the words in heart and soul, bind them on hand and forehead, teach them to their children, and write them on doorposts and gates. Finally, a blessing and a curse are set before them, to be placed on Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal once they cross the Jordan and possess the land.

l: the LORD your God, Deuteronomy, Chapter 11
s: The LORD your God is recalled as having done great works against Pharaoh and Egypt, drowning the Egyptian army in the Red Sea and causing the earth to swallow Dathan and Abiram. He cares for the promised land, with his eyes on it all year, and promises rain, grain, wine, oil, and grass for obedience. He will drive out greater nations and lay fear of Israel on the land, but will shut up the sky and let them perish if they serve other gods.

The Israelites are addressed as eyewitnesses of the LORD's works in Egypt, the Red Sea, and the wilderness, and are commanded to love him and keep all his commandments. They are told to bind the words on hand and forehead, teach them to their children, and write them on doorposts and gates. They are about to cross the Jordan to possess the land, and are warned that their heart might be deceived into serving other gods.

Egypt is remembered as the place where the LORD did signs and works against Pharaoh and all his land. Its army, horses, and chariots were overflowed by the Red Sea as they pursued Israel. Its land, where seed was watered by foot like a garden of herbs, is contrasted with the rain-fed land Israel will enter.

The land is described as a land of hills and valleys that drinks rain from the sky, flowing with milk and honey, and watched over by the LORD all year. It was sworn to Israel's fathers, and its nations are to be dispossessed, with borders from the wilderness and Lebanon to the Euphrates and the western sea. It lies beyond the Jordan, in the land of the Canaanites near Gilgal and the oaks of Moreh, and is the site for the blessing on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal.

l: commandments, statutes, and ordinances, Deuteronomy, Chapter 11
s: The commandments, statutes, and ordinances are to be kept always, so the Israelites may be strong, possess the land, and prolong their days. They are to be laid up in heart and soul, bound as a sign, taught to children, and written on doorposts and gates. Keeping them brings rain, fruitfulness, and victory over nations, while turning from them to other gods brings drought and perishing.

Moses sets before the Israelites a blessing for listening to the LORD's commandments and a curse for not listening and going after other gods. When they enter the land, the blessing is to be set on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal. These mountains are described as beyond the Jordan, in the land of the Canaanites near Gilgal and the oaks of Moreh.

In Chapter 12, the speaker instructs the Israelites on how to live in the land the LORD is giving them. They must utterly destroy the nations' worship sites, altars, pillars, Asherah poles and images, but must not worship the LORD in that way. Offerings, tithes, vows and sacrifices are to be brought only to the one place the LORD chooses, where the people and the Levite rejoice before him. Meat may be killed and eaten within their own gates, including when the chosen place is too far away, but the blood must never be eaten and must be poured out on the earth. The chapter ends with warnings not to imitate the nations' worship, which includes burning sons and daughters in fire, and not to add to or take away from the commands.

l: the LORD your God, Deuteronomy, Chapter 12
s: The LORD is the God of the fathers who gives the land to the Israelites and will give them rest from their enemies. He will choose one place in one of the tribes to put his name, and he commands that he not be worshiped as the nations worship their gods, since he hates their abominations.

The Israelites are commanded to destroy the nations' worship sites, bring their offerings only to the LORD's chosen place, and rejoice there with their households. They may eat meat at home but must not eat blood, must not forsake the Levite, must not imitate the nations' gods, and must neither add to nor take away from the commands.

l: nations of the land, Deuteronomy, Chapter 12
s: The nations will be dispossessed and cut off by the LORD before the Israelites, who will dwell in their land. Their worship sites are to be destroyed, and the Israelites are warned not to inquire after their gods, because the nations did every abomination the LORD hates, even burning their sons and daughters in fire.

The Levite lives within the Israelites' gates and has no portion or inheritance with them. He is to share in rejoicing and eating before the LORD at the chosen place, and the Israelites are told not to forsake him as long as they live in the land.

l: place the LORD shall choose, Deuteronomy, Chapter 12
s: The chosen place is the single location the LORD will choose among the tribes to put his name and make it dwell. All burnt offerings, sacrifices, tithes, wave offerings, vows and firstborn animals are to be brought and eaten there, not in every place the Israelites see.

l: pagan worship sites and objects, Deuteronomy, Chapter 12
s: The nations' places on high mountains, hills and under green trees are to be destroyed. Their altars are to be broken down, pillars dashed in pieces, Asherah poles burned and engraved images cut down, so that their name is destroyed from the place.

Burnt offerings, sacrifices, tithes, wave offerings, vows, free will offerings and firstborn of herd and flock must be brought to the chosen place and not offered anywhere else. The Israelites eat the eligible portions there before the LORD and rejoice. The blood and meat of burnt offerings are offered on the LORD's altar.

The Israelites may kill and eat meat within their gates as their desire leads, as with the gazelle and deer, and the clean and unclean may eat it alike. This permission holds when the border is enlarged or the chosen place is too far away, but it does not extend to the tithes, firstborn, vows and offerings, which must be eaten at the chosen place.

The Israelites are forbidden to eat blood because the blood is the life, and the life must not be eaten with the meat. It is to be poured out on the earth like water, and obedience is tied to things going well for them and their children. Blood from sacrifices is poured out on the LORD's altar.

Chapter 13 gives three laws about enticement to worship other gods. A prophet or dreamer of dreams who urges following other gods must not be heeded even if his sign comes true, because the LORD your God is testing Israel's love, and that prophet is to be put to death. A close relative or friend who secretly entices someone to serve other gods must not be pitied, spared, or concealed, and is to be stoned, with the hearer's hand first and then all the people's. If a city is reported to have been drawn away by wicked fellows, the people must investigate diligently, and if it is true they must strike down its inhabitants and livestock, burn the city with its plunder, and leave it a permanent heap. The chapter ends by promising that the LORD will turn from his anger and show mercy and multiplication if Israel keeps his commandments and takes nothing of the devoted thing.

l: the LORD your God, Deuteronomy, Chapter 13
s: The LORD your God is said to test Israel through a prophet whose sign comes true, to learn whether they love him with all their heart and soul. He is the one who brought Israel out of Egypt, the house of bondage, and he commands that those who lead people to other gods be put to death. If Israel destroys the idolatrous city and keeps the devoted thing from their hands, he will turn from his fierce anger, show mercy and compassion, and multiply them as he swore to their fathers.

l: prophet or dreamer of dreams, Deuteronomy, Chapter 13
s: A prophet or dreamer of dreams who gives a sign or wonder that comes to pass but says, "Let's go after other gods," is not to be listened to. He is to be put to death for speaking rebellion against the LORD, in order to remove evil from among the people.

The other gods are described as gods Israel and its fathers have not known, belonging to the peoples near and far, from one end of the earth to the other. Calls to go and serve them are the common element in all three cases: the prophet, the secret enticer, and the wicked fellows of a city.

Israel is commanded to walk after the LORD, fear him, keep his commandments, obey his voice, serve him, and cling to him. They are told to refuse any enticement to other gods, to carry out the death penalty without pity, and to investigate and destroy any city that turns away. All Israel is meant to hear and fear so that such wickedness is not done again among them.

l: secret enticer (close relative or friend), Deuteronomy, Chapter 13
s: A brother, son, daughter, wife, or friend as close as one's own soul who secretly urges serving other gods is not to be consented to, listened to, pitied, spared, or concealed. The person enticed must kill him, with his hand first on him and afterward the hands of all the people, by stoning, because he sought to draw them from the LORD.

If it is reported that wicked fellows from among the people have drawn the inhabitants of a city to serve other gods, the people must inquire, investigate, and ask diligently. If it is true, they are to strike the inhabitants and livestock with the sword, gather the plunder into the street, and burn the city with it as an offering to the LORD. It is to remain a heap forever and never be rebuilt, and nothing of the devoted thing may be kept.

l: death penalty for idolatry, Deuteronomy, Chapter 13
s: The chapter prescribes death for the prophet or dreamer who urges other gods, for the secret enticer who is a relative or friend, and for the inhabitants of a city that has been drawn away. The enticer is stoned with the accuser's hand first, and the city is struck by the sword and burned. The stated purposes are to remove evil from among the people and to make all Israel hear and fear.

Chapter 14 addresses the Israelites, called children of the LORD their God and a holy people chosen as his own possession, and forbids them to cut themselves or shave their foreheads for the dead. It lists which animals, fish, and birds may be eaten and which are unclean, including the camel, hare, rabbit, pig, creatures without fins and scales, and a long list of birds. It forbids eating anything that dies of itself, though it may be given or sold to a foreigner, and forbids boiling a young goat in its mother's milk. The chapter then commands tithing the yearly increase, to be eaten before the LORD in the place he chooses, or exchanged for money if the way is too far. Every third year the tithe is stored within the gates for the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow, so that the LORD may bless the work of the Israelites' hands.

l: the LORD your God, Deuteronomy, Chapter 14
s: The LORD your God is said to have chosen the Israelites as his own possession above all peoples on earth. He sets the rules on mourning, eating, and tithing, and chooses the place where his name dwells. He promises to bless the Israelites in all the work of their hands when they provide for the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow.

The Israelites are told they are children of the LORD and a holy people chosen for his own possession. They are forbidden to cut themselves or shave their foreheads for the dead, to eat abominable things, or to eat what dies of itself. They are commanded to tithe, to eat and rejoice before the LORD, and to care for the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow.

Clean animals may be eaten: those that part the hoof, have it split in two, and chew the cud, such as the ox, sheep, goat, deer, gazelle, roebuck, wild goat, ibex, antelope, and chamois. Of the waters, whatever has fins and scales is allowed, and all clean birds may be eaten.

Unclean animals include the camel, hare, and rabbit, which chew the cud but do not part the hoof, and the pig, which has a split hoof but does not chew the cud. Water creatures without fins and scales, many named birds (eagle, vulture, raven, owl, stork, bat and others), and all winged creeping things are also unclean and may not be eaten. The pig's carcass may not be touched.

The dietary laws permit animals that part the hoof and chew the cud, fish with fins and scales, and clean birds, and forbid the listed unclean animals and birds. They also forbid eating anything that dies of itself, though it may be given or sold to a foreigner. They forbid boiling a young goat in its mother's milk, and are grounded in Israel being a holy people.

The Israelites must tithe all the yearly increase of their seed, along with grain, new wine, oil, and the firstborn of herd and flock, eating it before the LORD so they learn to fear him. If the way is too far, it may be turned into money and exchanged at the chosen place for cattle, sheep, wine, or strong drink. Every third year the tithe is stored within the gates for the Levite, foreigner, fatherless, and widow.

l: place the LORD shall choose, Deuteronomy, Chapter 14
s: The place the LORD chooses is where he causes his name to dwell. The Israelites are to eat their tithe there before him and rejoice with their households. If it is too far, they carry money instead and buy what they desire when they arrive.

The Levite lives within the Israelites' gates and has no portion or inheritance with them. The Israelites are told not to forsake him. In the third year he comes with the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow to eat the stored tithe and be satisfied.

Chapter 15 gives Israelites commands from the LORD their God about debts, poverty, slaves, and firstborn animals. Every seventh year creditors must cancel debts owed by fellow Israelites, though they may still collect from a foreigner. Israelites are told to lend generously to a poor brother without a wicked or grieving heart, because the poor will never cease from the land. A Hebrew servant who has served six years must be freed in the seventh year and furnished liberally from flock, threshing floor, and wine press, remembering Israel's slavery in Egypt; a servant who loves his master may instead have his ear pierced with an awl and serve forever. Firstborn male animals are to be dedicated to the LORD and eaten yearly at the chosen place, unless defective, and their blood must be poured out on the ground.

l: the LORD your God, Deuteronomy, Chapter 15
s: The LORD your God promises to bless the Israelites in the land he gives them if they obey, including that they will lend to many nations and rule over them. He is the one who redeemed them from Egypt, and he will hear the cry of a poor brother who is refused help. He is the one to whom firstborn males are dedicated, and he will choose the place where they are eaten.

l: seventh-year release of debts, Deuteronomy, Chapter 15
s: At the end of every seven years, creditors must release what they lent to a fellow Israelite and not demand payment, because the LORD's release has been proclaimed. A foreigner may still be required to pay. The text warns against refusing to lend as the seventh year nears, since that would be sin.

l: creditor (the lender among the Israelites), Deuteronomy, Chapter 15
s: The creditor must release what he has lent to his neighbor and brother in the seventh year, though he may still require payment from a foreigner. He is told not to harden his heart or shut his hand toward a poor brother, to lend sufficient for the need, and not to hold back because the release year is near. He is to give without a grieving heart, because the LORD will bless him for it.

l: poor brother (the needy fellow Israelite), Deuteronomy, Chapter 15
s: The poor brother is to receive an open hand and a loan sufficient for his need, and must not be refused because the year of release is near. If refused, he may cry to the LORD against the lender, and it would be sin to the lender. The text says the poor will never cease out of the land.

l: Hebrew servant (the slave sold to a fellow Israelite), Deuteronomy, Chapter 15
s: A Hebrew man or woman sold to a fellow Israelite serves six years and goes free in the seventh, not empty-handed but liberally furnished from the master's flock, threshing floor, and wine press. If the servant says he will not leave because he loves the master and his house, the master pierces his ear with an awl to the door and he serves forever. The master is told the servant has been worth double a hired hand.

l: release of slaves in the seventh year, Deuteronomy, Chapter 15
s: In the seventh year a Hebrew servant who has served six years must be let go free, and the master must not send him away empty. The command is grounded in remembering that Israel was a slave in Egypt and the LORD redeemed them. The master should not find it hard, because the LORD will bless him in all he does.

l: firstborn of the herd and flock, Deuteronomy, Chapter 15
s: All firstborn males of the herd and flock are to be dedicated to the LORD, not worked or shorn. They are eaten year by year before the LORD in the place he chooses, by the owner and his household. An animal with any defect, such as lameness or blindness, must not be sacrificed; it is eaten within the gates by clean and unclean alike, and the blood is poured out on the ground like water.

The Israelites are commanded to cancel debts among themselves every seventh year, to give generously to the poor, and to free Hebrew servants with provisions after six years. They are promised blessing and rule over many nations if they obey. They are also told to dedicate firstborn animals, eat them at the chosen place, and not eat blood.

Chapter 16 gives the Israelites instructions for three annual festivals to be kept for the LORD their God at the place he will choose: Passover with the seven days of unleavened bread, the feast of weeks, and the feast of booths. It specifies how Passover is sacrificed and eaten, that all households including servants, Levites, foreigners, the fatherless, and widows rejoice, and that all males appear three times a year, each giving as able. The chapter then commands that judges and officers be appointed in every gate according to the tribes to judge with righteous judgment, without perverting justice, showing partiality, or taking bribes. It ends by forbidding an Asherah beside the LORD's altar and any sacred stone, which he hates.

l: the LORD your God, Deuteronomy, Chapter 16
s: The LORD your God brought Israel out of Egypt by night in the month of Abib and will choose a place to cause his name to dwell. He commands the three feasts, blesses the people in their increase, and gives them the land and gates. He hates sacred stones and forbids an Asherah beside his altar.

Passover is to be kept in the month of Abib to the LORD, sacrificed from the flock and herd at the chosen place at evening, at sunset, at the season of leaving Egypt. It is roasted and eaten there, none of the meat may remain until morning, and it may not be sacrificed within the people's own gates. The people return to their tents in the morning.

The Israelites are commanded to keep Passover, unleavened bread, weeks, and booths, rejoicing with their households, Levites, foreigners, the fatherless, and widows. All males appear before the LORD three times a year, giving as able, and they are to remember they were slaves in Egypt. They must also appoint judges, judge justly, and avoid the Asherah and sacred stones so that they may live and inherit the land.

l: feast of unleavened bread, Deuteronomy, Chapter 16
s: Unleavened bread is eaten for seven days with Passover as the bread of affliction, recalling the haste of leaving Egypt. No yeast is to be seen in their borders, and the seventh day is a solemn assembly with no work. It is one of the three feasts at which males appear before the LORD.

The feast of weeks comes after counting seven weeks from when the sickle is first put to the standing grain. It is kept with a free will offering given according to the LORD's blessing, and with rejoicing before him at the chosen place by the whole household, Levite, foreigner, fatherless, and widow. It is one of the three feasts at which males appear.

The feast of booths is kept seven days after the gathering in from the threshing floor and wine press. It is kept at the place the LORD chooses, with all in the household, the Levite, foreigner, fatherless, and widow rejoicing, because the LORD will bless their increase. It is the third of the feasts at which males appear.

l: place the LORD shall choose, Deuteronomy, Chapter 16
s: This is the place where the LORD will cause his name to dwell. Passover must be sacrificed and eaten there rather than within the people's gates, and the feasts are kept and males appear before him there. It is also where the people rejoice together.

Judges and officers are to be made in all the gates the LORD gives, according to the tribes. They are to judge the people with righteous judgment, not perverting justice, showing partiality, or taking bribes.

Justice is to be followed in full: it must not be perverted, partiality must not be shown, and bribes must not be taken because they blind the wise and pervert the words of the righteous. Following what is altogether just is tied to living and inheriting the land the LORD gives.

Chapter 17 sets out rules for worship, justice, and kingship in Israel. Sacrifices of defective oxen or sheep are forbidden as an abomination to the LORD. Anyone, man or woman, who serves other gods or the sun, moon, or stars must be diligently investigated and, if the charge is certain, stoned at the gates on the testimony of two or three witnesses, with the witnesses casting the first stones. Cases too hard for local judgment are to be taken to the Levitical priests and the judge at the place the LORD chooses, and their verdict must be followed without turning right or left, on pain of death. When the people later ask for a king, they must set over them the one the LORD chooses, from among their brothers, who must not multiply horses, wives, silver, or gold, and must write and read his own copy of the law all his life.

l: the LORD your God, Deuteronomy, Chapter 17
s: The LORD your God calls sacrifices of defective animals an abomination and forbids service of other gods. He chooses the place for judgment and chooses the king who may be set over the people. He has said the people must not go back to Egypt, and he gives the land they will possess.

Israel is the community in which abominations such as idolatry must be investigated and the evil removed. Those who presume to disobey the priest or judge are to be put away from it. It is also the land and people over which a king chosen by the LORD may eventually reign, with his descendants prolonging their days in the middle of it.

The Levitical priests, with the judge, give verdicts on cases too hard for local courts at the place the LORD chooses. Their decisions and teaching must be obeyed without deviation, and a man who presumptuously refuses to listen to the priest who ministers there is to die. They also hold the law from which the king is to copy his own book.

The judge who serves in those days sits with the priests at the chosen place and gives verdicts on hard cases brought up from the gates. His sentence must be followed without turning right or left, and presumptuous disobedience to him is punishable by death.

The king is to be one the LORD chooses from among the people's brothers, never a foreigner. He must not multiply horses, wives, silver, or gold, nor cause the people to return to Egypt. He must write his own copy of the law from the Levitical priests' book and read it all his life, so that he fears the LORD, keeps the law, and is not lifted up above his brothers, thereby prolonging his days and his children's in his kingdom.

The people are to inquire diligently into reported idolatry and carry out the stoning at the gates, with the witnesses first and then all the people. They are to take hard cases to the chosen place and obey the verdict, and they will hear and fear and not act presumptuously. When they possess the land and ask for a king like the nations around them, they are told to set over themselves the one the LORD chooses.

l: idolater (man or woman who serves other gods), Deuteronomy, Chapter 17
s: A man or woman who transgresses the covenant by serving and worshiping other gods, or the sun, moon, or stars, is to be investigated once the matter is reported. If the charge is true and certain, that person is brought out to the gates and stoned to death. This is done to remove the evil from among the people.

Two or three witnesses are required to put a person to death; one witness is not enough. The witnesses' hands are to be first on the condemned person, followed afterward by the hands of all the people.

The law is to be taught by the Levitical priests and followed without turning right or left. The king must copy it into a book from the priests' copy and read it all his life to learn to fear the LORD and keep its words and statutes. Keeping it is tied to the king not being lifted up above his brothers and to long reigns for him and his children.

l: hard cases in judgment, Deuteronomy, Chapter 17
s: Matters too hard to decide locally, such as between blood and blood, plea and plea, or stroke and stroke, are to be taken up to the place the LORD chooses. There the Levitical priests and the judge give a verdict that must be followed exactly. Anyone who presumptuously ignores it is to die.

Chapter 18 describes the provision for the priests and Levites, who have no tribal inheritance because the LORD himself is their inheritance, and lists the portions the people must give them. It also allows any Levite who comes to the chosen place to minister there and receive equal portions. The chapter then forbids Israel from imitating the abominations of the nations in the land, naming practices such as passing children through fire, divination, sorcery, and necromancy, which are the reason the LORD drives those nations out. It promises that the LORD will raise up a prophet like the speaker from among Israel's brothers, in answer to the people's request at Horeb not to hear the LORD's voice or see the fire again. Finally, it sets the penalty of death for a prophet who speaks presumptuously or in the name of other gods, and gives a test: a prophecy that does not come to pass was not spoken by the LORD.

l: the LORD your God, Deuteronomy, Chapter 18
s: The LORD is the inheritance of the Levites and receives offerings made by fire, and he chooses the Levites to minister in his name and the place of worship. He drives out the nations because of their abominations, will raise up a prophet like Moses and put his words in that prophet's mouth, and will hold accountable anyone who does not listen to him.

The Levites, the whole tribe of Levi, receive no portion or inheritance with Israel and live on the LORD's offerings. A Levite who comes from any town to the chosen place with all the desire of his soul may minister there like his fellow Levites and receive equal portions of food, in addition to what comes from the sale of his family possessions.

Israel is told to give the priests their due, including first fruits, and not to imitate the abominations of the nations when it enters the land. The people are to be blameless before the LORD, to listen to the coming prophet, and to recognize false prophecy by whether it comes to pass, without fearing the false prophet.

Moses, the speaker, recalls the people's request at Horeb not to hear the LORD's voice or see the great fire again, lest they die. He reports that the LORD approved what they said and promised to raise up a prophet like him.

l: prophet (the coming prophet like Moses), Deuteronomy, Chapter 18
s: The LORD promises to raise up this prophet from among Israel's brothers, like Moses, and to put his words in his mouth so that he speaks all that the LORD commands. Israel must listen to him, and the LORD will require an account from anyone who refuses.

A prophet who speaks presumptuously in the LORD's name something the LORD has not commanded, or who speaks in the name of other gods, shall die. The test given is that if the thing he speaks does not follow or happen, the LORD did not speak it, and Israel need not fear him.

The priests' due from those who sacrifice an ox or sheep is the shoulder, the two cheeks, and the inner parts. They also receive the first fruits of grain, new wine, and oil, and the first of the sheep's fleece.

l: nations of the land, Deuteronomy, Chapter 18
s: The nations Israel will dispossess practice abominations and listen to sorcerers and diviners. Because of these abominations, the LORD drives them out from before Israel.

Practices listed as forbidden include making a son or daughter pass through the fire, divination, fortune-telling, enchanting, sorcery, charming, consulting a familiar spirit, wizardry, and necromancy. Whoever does them is an abomination to the LORD, and Israel is not allowed to do them.

Chapter 19 sets out laws for Israel once the LORD your God gives them the land. Three cities of refuge are to be set apart so that a man slayer who killed a neighbor unintentionally, with no prior hatred, can flee there and live, safe from the avenger of blood; three more are to be added if the border is enlarged. A man who hates his neighbor, lies in wait, and kills him is to be taken from the city by the elders and handed to the avenger of blood to die. The chapter also forbids moving a neighbor's landmark, requires two or three witnesses to establish a matter, and prescribes that a false witness suffer the penalty he intended for his brother, following the principle of life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot.

l: the LORD your God, Deuteronomy, Chapter 19
s: The LORD your God gives the land to Israel, cuts off the nations before them, and commands that three cities be set apart, with three more to be added if he enlarges the border as he swore to their fathers and they keep his commandment to love him and walk in his ways. Disputes over false testimony are to be brought to stand before him, along with the priests and judges.

l: three cities of refuge, Deuteronomy, Chapter 19
s: Three cities are to be set apart in the middle of the land, with roads prepared and the land divided into three parts so every man slayer can flee to one. Three more are to be added if the border is enlarged, so that innocent blood is not shed and blood guilt does not fall on the people.

The man slayer who kills his neighbor unintentionally, having not hated him before, may flee to one of the cities and live, as in the example of an ax head slipping from its handle while chopping wood. This protects him from being pursued and killed though he is not worthy of death.

l: neighbor (of the man slayer), Deuteronomy, Chapter 19
s: The neighbor is the one killed, either accidentally, as when an ax head flies off the handle in the forest, or deliberately by someone who hated him and lay in wait. The text also commands that his landmark, set by those of old, not be removed.

The avenger of blood might pursue a man slayer in hot anger and kill him on the long road, though the man was not worthy of death, which is why the cities of refuge are provided. If the killer was a deliberate murderer, the elders deliver him into the avenger's hand to die.

The man who hates his neighbor, lies in wait, rises up against him, and strikes him mortally gets no protection by fleeing to a city of refuge. The elders of his city are to send for him and hand him to the avenger of blood to die, with no pity, purging innocent blood from Israel.

The land is what the LORD your God gives Israel to possess and inherit, and it is to be divided into three parts for the cities of refuge. Innocent blood must not be shed in it, and neighbors' ancient landmarks in the inheritance must not be removed.
One witness alone cannot rise against a man for any iniquity or sin; a matter must be established by the mouth of two or three witnesses.

An unrighteous witness who testifies wrongdoing against someone is brought before the LORD, the priests, and the judges, who inquire diligently. If he is found to have testified falsely against his brother, he receives the penalty he intended for him, so that the evil is removed and others fear to repeat it.

The chapter closes with the principle that the eye shall not pity: life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot. It is applied here to the false witness, who is to suffer what he planned for his brother.

Chapter 20 gives Israel rules for warfare. Before battle the priest tells the people not to fear because the LORD their God, who brought them out of Egypt, goes with them to fight for them. The officers then exempt men who have built an undedicated house, planted a vineyard not yet used, pledged to marry a woman not yet taken, or who are fearful and faint-hearted, and afterward appoint army captains. Distant cities must first be offered peace: if they accept they become forced laborers, and if they refuse they are besieged, their males killed, and women, children, livestock and plunder taken. The cities of the Hittites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites must be utterly destroyed so Israel is not taught their abominations, and during sieges fruit-bearing trees must be spared while non-food trees may be cut for bulwarks.

l: the LORD your God, Deuteronomy, Chapter 20
s: The LORD your God, who brought Israel out of Egypt, is said to go with the people to fight for them and save them. He delivers besieged cities into their hand and gives them plunder and an inheritance of cities. He has commanded the utter destruction of the Hittite, Amorite, Canaanite, Perizzite, Hivite and Jebusite peoples.

Israel is addressed as the people going out to battle, told not to fear larger forces with horses and chariots. They are to offer peace to cities, besiege those that refuse, and destroy the peoples of the inherited cities completely. They are to spare fruit trees during sieges.
Israel's enemies may have horses, chariots and greater numbers, yet Israel is told not to be afraid of them. The LORD goes with Israel to fight against them and save Israel.

l: priest (who addresses Israel before battle), Deuteronomy, Chapter 20
s: The priest approaches the people as they draw near to battle and tells them to hear, not to let their hearts faint, and not to fear or tremble. He assures them that the LORD goes with them to fight for them and save them.

l: officers (who address the people), Deuteronomy, Chapter 20
s: The officers speak to the people announcing exemptions for those with a new undedicated house, an unused vineyard, a betrothed but untaken wife, or a fearful and faint heart. When they finish, they appoint captains of armies at the head of the people.

Battle is the occasion for which Israel is prepared by the priest's encouragement and the officers' exemptions. Men could die in it, which is why some are sent home, and captains are appointed to lead the people once the speeches end.

Four groups may return home: a man who has built a house and not dedicated it, one who has planted a vineyard and not used its fruit, one pledged to a wife and not yet married, and the fearful and faint-hearted. The reasons given are that another man would otherwise dedicate the house, use the fruit or take the wife, and that a fearful man's fear would melt his brother's heart.

A city Israel approaches must first be offered peace. If it answers peacefully and opens, its people become forced laborers; if it makes war, it is besieged, and when delivered all its males are struck with the sword and its women, children, livestock and plunder taken. Bulwarks are built against it until it falls.

Cities very far from Israel and not among the nations' cities are treated under the peace-or-siege rule. If they refuse peace and fall, their males are killed and the women, little ones, livestock and plunder are taken by Israel.

l: cities of the nations of Canaan, Deuteronomy, Chapter 20
s: The cities of the Hittite, Amorite, Canaanite, Perizzite, Hivite and Jebusite peoples, which the LORD gives Israel as an inheritance, are to be utterly destroyed with nothing that breathes left alive. The stated reason is to keep Israel from learning their abominations done for their gods and sinning against the LORD.

Fruit trees near a besieged city are not to be destroyed with an ax because Israel may eat from them. The text asks whether the tree of the field is a man that it should be besieged. Only trees known not to be food trees may be cut down for building bulwarks.

Chapter 21 gives several laws for Israel in the land the LORD gives. When a slain man is found in a field and the killer is unknown, the elders of the nearest city must break the neck of an unworked heifer in an unplowed valley with running water, wash their hands over it, and declare their innocence so the blood is forgiven. A man who takes a beautiful captive woman as wife must let her shave her head, change her clothes, and mourn her parents a month, and if he no longer delights in her he must let her go free rather than sell her. A man with two wives must give the double portion to the firstborn son even if that son is the hated wife's. A stubborn, rebellious, gluttonous and drunken son is brought by his parents to the elders and stoned by the men of the city, and a man put to death and hanged on a tree must be buried the same day.

l: the LORD your God, Deuteronomy, Chapter 21
s: The LORD gives Israel the land to possess and delivers enemies into their hands in battle. He has chosen the priests, the sons of Levi, to minister to him and bless in his name, and he is asked to forgive his redeemed people Israel and not allow innocent blood among them. The land is his gift, which must not be defiled by leaving a hanged body overnight.

l: slain man (found in the field), Deuteronomy, Chapter 21
s: He is found dead in a field in the land, and it is not known who struck him. The elders measure from him to the surrounding cities to determine the nearest one, which then bears responsibility for the ritual.

l: elders of the nearest city, Deuteronomy, Chapter 21
s: The elders of the city nearest the slain man take an unworked heifer to a valley with running water and break its neck. They wash their hands over it and declare that their hands did not shed the blood nor their eyes see it, and ask forgiveness for Israel. The blood is then forgiven them.

The heifer must be from the herd, never worked and never drawn in a yoke. The elders bring it to an unplowed, unsown valley with running water, where its neck is broken, and they wash their hands over it.

Israel is the people the LORD has redeemed and who are to put away innocent blood by doing what is right in his eyes. They are given laws on unsolved killing, captive wives, inheritance, a rebellious son, and burial of the hanged. All Israel is to hear of the rebellious son's punishment and fear.

l: heifer ritual for unsolved murder, Deuteronomy, Chapter 21
s: When a slain man is found and the killer unknown, the elders and judges measure to the nearest city, whose elders break an unworked heifer's neck in an uncultivated valley with running water. The priests come near, the elders wash their hands and make their declaration and prayer, and the blood is forgiven, putting away innocent blood.

A beautiful woman taken captive in battle may be brought into her captor's house as his wife. She must shave her head, trim her nails, take off her captive's clothing, and mourn her father and mother a full month. If he has no delight in her he must let her go where she desires, not sell her or treat her as a slave, because he has humbled her.

A man who goes to battle and sees a beautiful captive woman he desires may take her as his wife after she has mourned a month. If he later has no delight in her, he must let her go free and may not sell her for money or deal with her as a slave.

l: man with two wives, Deuteronomy, Chapter 21
s: He has one beloved wife and one hated wife, both of whom have borne him sons. When he divides his inheritance, he may not give the beloved wife's son the firstborn's rights over the hated wife's firstborn, but must acknowledge the true firstborn.
She is the less-loved of a man's two wives and has borne him children, including his firstborn son. Her status does not change her son's right as firstborn.

l: firstborn son of the hated wife, Deuteronomy, Chapter 21
s: Though his mother is the hated wife, he is the firstborn and his father must acknowledge him as such. He is called the beginning of his father's strength, and the right of the firstborn is his.

l: firstborn's double portion inheritance, Deuteronomy, Chapter 21
s: The father must give the acknowledged firstborn a double portion of all he has. This applies even when the firstborn is the son of the hated wife, and it may not be given instead to the beloved wife's son.

l: stubborn and rebellious son, Deuteronomy, Chapter 21
s: He will not obey his father or mother and does not listen even when they chasten him. His parents bring him to the elders at the city gate, accusing him of being stubborn, rebellious, a glutton and a drunkard. All the men of his city then stone him to death, removing the evil from among them.

l: parents of the rebellious son, Deuteronomy, Chapter 21
s: After chastening fails, the father and mother take hold of their son and bring him to the elders of his city at the gate. They state that he is stubborn, rebellious, will not obey, and is a glutton and drunkard.

l: man put to death and hanged, Deuteronomy, Chapter 21
s: A man who has committed a sin worthy of death may be put to death and hanged on a tree. His body must not remain overnight but must be buried the same day, for he who is hanged is accursed of God, and leaving him would defile the land.

Chapter 22 gives a series of commands about neighborly duty, purity, and sexual conduct. The addressee must return a brother's straying ox, sheep, donkey, garment or any lost item, and must help lift a fallen animal. Further rules cover cross-dressing, taking a hen with her young, a roof railing, mixed seed, mixed plowing, mixed cloth, and cloak fringes. The longest section handles a husband who falsely accuses his new wife of lacking virginity: her parents present the tokens before the elders, who punish a false accuser with chastisement, a hundred-shekel fine and a ban on divorce, while a proven charge means the young lady is stoned. The chapter ends with rulings on adultery, a betrothed virgin in the city versus the field, an unbetrothed virgin seized by a man, and a ban on taking one's father's wife.

l: father of the young lady, Deuteronomy, Chapter 22
s: The young lady's father, with her mother, brings the tokens of her virginity to the elders at the gate and states that he gave his daughter to the man, who now hates her. If the accusation is proved false, he receives the fine of one hundred shekels. In the case of an unbetrothed virgin seized, he receives fifty shekels from the man.

l: elders of the city, Deuteronomy, Chapter 22
s: The elders of the city sit at the gate and hear the dispute over the accused wife. The cloth is spread before them. If the husband is found false, they take him and chastise him and fine him one hundred shekels of silver.

The tokens of virginity are the cloth the young lady's parents bring and spread before the elders to refute the husband's charge. Their presence clears her and condemns him. If they were not found in her, she is stoned.

l: adultery with a married woman (case), Deuteronomy, Chapter 22
s: If a man is found lying with a woman married to a husband, both the man and the woman must die. This removes the evil from Israel.

l: man and betrothed virgin in the city (case), Deuteronomy, Chapter 22
s: If a man finds a betrothed virgin in the city and lies with her, both are brought to the city gate and stoned. She dies because she did not cry out in the city, and he because he humbled his neighbor's wife. This removes the evil from among them.

l: rape of a betrothed woman in the field (case), Deuteronomy, Chapter 22
s: If a man finds a betrothed lady in the field and forces her, only the man dies. She is to be left unpunished, having no sin worthy of death, because she cried out and no one was there to save her. The case is compared to a man rising against his neighbor and killing him.
If a man grabs an unbetrothed virgin and lies with her and they are found, he must give her father fifty shekels of silver. She becomes his wife because he humbled her, and he may never put her away.

Chapter 23 gives laws for the Israelites on who may enter the LORD's assembly, excluding those emasculated by crushing or cutting, those born of a forbidden union, and Ammonites and Moabites, who are barred because they withheld bread and water and hired Balaam to curse Israel, while Edomites and Egyptians are not to be abhorred and their third-generation children may enter. It then sets rules for keeping the military camp holy, including removing uncleanness and burying excrement, because the LORD walks in the middle of the camp. It forbids returning an escaped servant to his master, forbids prostitution among Israelites and the use of prostitutes' wages in the LORD's house, and forbids lending to a brother on interest while permitting it to a foreigner. It closes by requiring that vows to the LORD be paid, and by allowing a person in a neighbor's vineyard or grain field to eat grapes or pluck ears by hand but not carry grapes away in a container or use a sickle.

l: the LORD your God, Deuteronomy, Chapter 23
s: The LORD is the one whose assembly is restricted, who turned Balaam's curse into a blessing because he loved Israel, and who walks in the middle of the camp to deliver the Israelites and give up their enemies. He requires a holy camp, hates the wages of prostitution brought into his house, blesses those who do not charge their brother interest, and will surely require vows made to him.

The Israelites are commanded in this unit to exclude certain people from the assembly, not to abhor Edomites or Egyptians, to keep their camp clean and holy, and to shelter escaped servants without oppressing them. They are also told to avoid prostitution, not to charge a brother interest (though they may charge a foreigner), to pay their vows, and to limit what they take from a neighbor's vineyard or grain.

The LORD's assembly is closed to the emasculated, to those born of a forbidden union, and to Ammonites and Moabites, with the restriction lasting to the tenth generation. The children of Edomites and Egyptians may enter in the third generation.

Ammonites are barred from the LORD's assembly even to the tenth generation, forever, because they did not meet Israel with bread and water on the way out of Egypt and hired Balaam to curse them. The Israelites are told not to seek their peace or prosperity all their days.

Moabites are barred from the LORD's assembly even to the tenth generation, forever, for not meeting Israel with bread and water and for hiring Balaam the son of Beor to curse them. The Israelites are told not to seek their peace or prosperity all their days.

When the Israelites camp against enemies, they must keep from every evil thing. A man made unclean by a nighttime emission must stay outside until evening, bathe, and return at sundown, and waste must be relieved outside the camp and covered with a trowel, so the camp stays holy because the LORD walks in it.

A servant who has escaped from his master to the Israelites must not be handed back to the master. He is to live among them in the place of his choosing within one of their gates, where it pleases him best, and he is not to be oppressed.

No Israelite daughter or son is to be a prostitute, and the hire of a prostitute or the wages of a male prostitute must not be brought into the LORD's house for any vow. Both are called an abomination to the LORD.

Israelites may not lend to a brother on interest, whether of money, food, or anything else lent on interest. They may charge a foreigner interest, and obeying the rule on brothers is tied to the LORD's blessing in the land.

A vow to the LORD must be paid without delay, since he will surely require it and failing to pay is sin. Not making a vow is no sin, and whatever one has promised as a free will offering must be done.

l: neighbor's vineyard and grain, Deuteronomy, Chapter 23
s: A person entering a neighbor's vineyard may eat his fill of grapes but may not put any in a container. A person in a neighbor's standing grain may pluck ears by hand but may not use a sickle.

Chapter 24 gives laws on marriage, divorce, and justice toward the vulnerable. A man who finds something unseemly in his wife may give her a certificate of divorce, and if she remarries and is divorced or widowed, her first husband may not take her again, as that is an abomination to the LORD. A newly married man is exempt from the army and business for one year to cheer his wife. Other laws forbid taking a mill as a pledge, require returning a poor man's garment pledge by sundown, prohibit kidnapping and enslaving fellow Israelites (a death penalty), and command prompt daily payment of poor hired servants. The chapter ends by forbidding the perversion of justice for foreigners, the fatherless, and widows, and by leaving forgotten sheaves, olives, and grapes for them, recalling Israel's slavery in Egypt.

l: the LORD your God, Deuteronomy, Chapter 24
s: The LORD declares that a former husband remarrying a divorced wife after she has been defiled is an abomination and would cause the land to sin. He gave the land as an inheritance, taught the Levitical priests how to handle leprosy, and punished Miriam. He redeemed Israel from slavery in Egypt, which is the basis for commands to act justly, and he blesses those who return pledges and leave gleanings.

l: husband (the man who divorces his wife), Deuteronomy, Chapter 24
s: A husband who finds some unseemly thing in his wife may write her a certificate of divorce, put it in her hand, and send her out of his house. If she later marries another man and is divorced or widowed, he may not take her again as wife. A newly married man is exempt from the army and business for one year to cheer his wife.

The wife who finds no favor is given a certificate of divorce and sent out of the house. After leaving she may become another man's wife. If her second husband divorces her or dies, she is considered defiled with respect to her first husband, who may not take her back.

Divorce is done by writing a certificate, placing it in the wife's hand, and sending her from the house. It frees her to marry another man. If a second marriage ends by divorce or death, the first husband may not remarry her, since that is an abomination to the LORD.

Pledges are regulated: no one may take a mill or upper millstone because it takes a life in pledge, and a widow's clothing may not be taken. A lender may not enter the borrower's house to get it, and must wait outside. A poor man's pledge garment must be returned by sundown so he can sleep in it and bless the lender, which counts as righteousness.

The lender must not enter the neighbor's house to get a pledge but stand outside while the borrower brings it. He must not sleep with a poor man's pledge and must return it at sundown. Doing so is righteousness before the LORD.

The neighbor who borrows brings the pledge outside to the lender rather than having his house entered. If poor, he gets his garment pledge back at sundown so he may sleep in it. He then blesses the lender.

A poor and needy hired servant, whether a brother or a foreigner within the gates, must not be oppressed. He must be paid his wages on the same day before sunset because he sets his heart on them. Otherwise he may cry out to the LORD against the employer, and it would be sin.

The foreigner is protected from being deprived of justice and is counted among poor hired servants who must be paid promptly. Forgotten sheaves, olive boughs, and vineyard gleanings are left for him. Israel is told to remember it was a slave in Egypt.

The fatherless must not be deprived of justice. Sheaves forgotten in the field, olives remaining on the boughs, and vineyard gleanings are left for them. The commands are grounded in Israel's memory of slavery in Egypt.

A widow's clothing may not be taken in pledge, and she must not be deprived of justice. Forgotten sheaves, remaining olives, and vineyard gleanings are left for her. The LORD will bless the work of those who do so.

l: gleaning harvest (sheaf, olives, vineyard), Deuteronomy, Chapter 24
s: A sheaf forgotten in the field must not be fetched again, olive boughs must not be gone over a second time, and the vineyard must not be gleaned after the harvest. All of it is left for the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow. The LORD promises to bless the work of the owner's hands for this.

Chapter 25 sets out several laws for Israel. Judges are to justify the righteous and condemn the wicked, and a wicked man sentenced to a beating may receive no more than forty stripes so that he is not degraded. The ox treading grain must not be muzzled. When a man dies without a son, his brother must marry the widow so the dead man's name is not blotted out of Israel; if the surviving brother refuses, the widow brings the matter to the elders, removes his sandal, and spits in his face, and his house is given a shameful name. The chapter also commands cutting off the hand of a woman who grabs a man's private parts while he fights her husband, forbids diverse weights and measures as an abomination to the LORD, and ends with the command to remember what Amalek did to the feeble rearmost Israelites and, once given rest, to blot out Amalek's memory.

l: the LORD your God, Deuteronomy, Chapter 25
s: The LORD your God gives Israel the land and promises long days to those who keep honest weights and measures. He regards all who act unrighteously as an abomination, and he commands that, once he has given rest from enemies, the memory of Amalek be blotted out.

Amalek met Israel on the way out of Egypt and struck the rearmost, the feeble ones, when they were faint and weary, and he did not fear God. Israel is commanded to remember this and, when given rest from its enemies, to blot out Amalek's memory from under the sky.

Israel receives laws on judicial beatings capped at forty stripes, the ox not being muzzled, levirate duty, punishment for a woman's act in a fight, and honest weights and measures. It is told that a dead man's name must not be blotted out of Israel, that a refusing brother's house will be named in Israel, and that it must remember and blot out Amalek.

When brothers dwell together and one dies without a son, his widow must not marry a stranger; her husband's brother is to take her as wife and perform a husband's brother's duty. Her firstborn son succeeds in the dead man's name so that it is not blotted out of Israel.
The brother who dies without a son is to have his name preserved in Israel through the firstborn son born to his widow and his brother. This son succeeds in his name so it will not be blotted out.

The widow of a man who died childless must not be married outside to a stranger. If her husband's brother refuses her, she goes to the elders at the gate, states his refusal, and before the elders removes his sandal and spits in his face.

The surviving brother is obligated to take his dead brother's widow as wife. If he refuses and persists after the elders speak to him, he has his sandal loosed and is spat on by her, and his house is called 'The house of him who had his sandal removed.'

The ritual is performed when a surviving brother refuses levirate duty: the widow, before the elders, loosens his sandal from his foot and spits in his face, saying that this is done to the man who does not build up his brother's house. It leaves his house with a shameful name in Israel.

l: honest weights and measures, Deuteronomy, Chapter 25
s: Israel is forbidden to keep diverse weights in the bag or diverse measures in the house, one heavy and one light, one large and one small. It must keep perfect and just ones so its days may be long in the land, since all who act unrighteously are an abomination to the LORD.

Chapter 26 instructs the Israelites, once they possess and dwell in the land the LORD gives them, to bring the first of the ground's fruit in a basket to the place the LORD chooses. There they give it to the priest, who sets it before the altar, and they recite a confession recounting their father the Syrian, the Egyptian oppression, and the LORD's deliverance and gift of a land flowing with milk and honey. They are to rejoice with the Levite and the foreigner. In the third year, the year of tithing, they give the tithe to the Levite, foreigner, fatherless, and widow, then declare before the LORD that they have obeyed and ask for his blessing. The chapter closes with the LORD commanding them to keep his statutes and ordinances, and with the mutual declaration that they are his people and he is their God, who will set them high above all nations.

l: the LORD your God, Deuteronomy, Chapter 26
s: The LORD gives the land as an inheritance and chooses the place where his name dwells. He is recalled as having heard the cries of the people, seen their affliction, and brought them out of Egypt with a mighty hand, an outstretched arm, great terror, signs, and wonders. He commands them to keep his statutes and ordinances, declares them his own possession, and promises to make them high above all nations in praise, name, and honor.

They are told to bring the first of their fruit in a basket to the chosen place, recite a confession of their history, worship, and rejoice. In the third year they must give the tithe to the Levite, foreigner, fatherless, and widow, and declare their obedience. They declare the LORD to be their God and are declared his own people, called to be a holy people who keep all his commandments.

The priest serving in those days receives the worshipper's profession that he has come into the promised land. He takes the basket from the worshipper's hand and sets it down before the altar of the LORD.

Some of the first of all the ground's fruit is to be put in a basket and carried to the place the LORD chooses. The priest sets it before the altar, and the worshipper recites a confession, sets it down, and worships. It is followed by rejoicing in the good the LORD has given, shared with the Levite and the foreigner.

The land is described as the LORD's gift and inheritance, sworn to the fathers, and a land flowing with milk and honey. The Israelites are to possess it and dwell in it, and the fruit of its ground is the source of the offering. The worshipper's confession acknowledges that the LORD has brought them into it, and the people ask for blessing on the ground.

Egypt is where the worshipper's father, a Syrian ready to perish, went down and lived, few in number, and became a great, mighty, and populous nation. The Egyptians mistreated and afflicted the people and imposed hard labor. The LORD brought the people out of Egypt with a mighty hand, an outstretched arm, great terror, signs, and wonders.

l: tithe of the third year, Deuteronomy, Chapter 26
s: In the third year, called the year of tithing, the people finish tithing all their increase and give it to the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow, so that they may eat within the gates and be filled. The giver then declares before the LORD that he has put away the holy things, not eaten of it in mourning, not removed it while unclean, and not given of it for the dead.

Moses and the elders of Israel command the people to set up large plastered stones on Mount Ebal after crossing the Jordan, inscribe all the words of the law on them, and build an altar of uncut stones for burnt and peace offerings. Moses and the Levitical priests then tell Israel to be silent and listen, declaring that today they have become the people of the LORD their God and must obey his commandments. Moses assigns six tribes (Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph, Benjamin) to stand on Mount Gerizim for the blessing and six (Reuben, Gad, Asher, Zebulun, Dan, Naphtali) on Mount Ebal for the curse. The Levites are to declare a series of curses, covering secret idolatry, dishonoring parents, moving a neighbor's landmark, misleading the blind, withholding justice from the foreigner, fatherless and widow, various sexual offenses, secret murder, taking a bribe to kill the innocent, and failing to uphold the law, and all the people answer 'Amen' to each.

Moses, together with the elders of Israel, commands the people to set up plastered stones inscribed with the law and to build an altar on Mount Ebal after crossing the Jordan. He and the Levitical priests tell Israel they have become the LORD's people and must obey him, and he assigns the twelve tribes to stand on Gerizim for blessing or Ebal for the curse.

Israel is told to cross the Jordan, set up inscribed stones and an altar on Mount Ebal, and hear that today they have become the people of the LORD their God. The tribes are divided between Mounts Gerizim and Ebal, and all the people are to answer 'Amen' to each curse the Levites pronounce.

l: the LORD your God, Deuteronomy, Chapter 27
s: The LORD is the God of Israel who gives them the land and who is to be honored with an altar of uncut stones, burnt offerings, and peace offerings with rejoicing before him. Israel is declared to be his people and is commanded to obey his voice, commandments, and statutes. He had promised the land to their fathers.

Mount Ebal is the place where Israel is to set up the plastered stones inscribed with the law and build the LORD's altar of uncut stones. It is also where the tribes of Reuben, Gad, Asher, Zebulun, Dan, and Naphtali are to stand for the curse.
Mount Gerizim is the mountain where the tribes of Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph, and Benjamin are to stand to bless the people after crossing the Jordan.

The land is described as the one the LORD gives Israel, a land flowing with milk and honey, as he promised their fathers. Israel is to enter it after passing over the Jordan, and the commanded stones and altar are to be set up once they have crossed.

The Levitical priests join Moses in telling Israel to be silent and listen because they have become the LORD's people. The Levites are also to say the curses aloud to all the men of Israel, with the people responding 'Amen'.

l: plastered stones (stones inscribed with the law), Deuteronomy, Chapter 27
s: Great stones are to be set up on Mount Ebal after Israel crosses the Jordan and coated with plaster. All the words of the law are to be written on them very plainly.

The law is to be written in full, very plainly, on plastered stones on Mount Ebal. The final curse pronounces a curse on anyone who does not uphold its words by doing them, and the people answer 'Amen'.

l: altar (altar to the LORD on Mount Ebal), Deuteronomy, Chapter 27
s: Israel is to build an altar to the LORD on Mount Ebal from uncut stones, using no iron tool on them. Burnt offerings are to be made on it and peace offerings sacrificed, with the people eating there and rejoicing before the LORD.

Twelve curses are to be declared by the Levites in a loud voice, covering secret idolatry, dishonoring parents, moving a landmark, leading the blind astray, withholding justice from the foreigner, fatherless, and widow, several sexual offenses, secret murder, taking a bribe to kill the innocent, and not upholding the law. The people are to answer 'Amen' after each one.

Chapter 28 is a speech addressed to the Israelites, in which the LORD's commandments are tied to blessings for obedience and curses for disobedience. Verses 1-14 promise blessings in city, field, family, livestock, harvest, and battle, and say the people will be set high above all nations as head and not tail. Verses 15-57 give a much longer list of curses: confusion, disease, drought, defeat, loss of family and property, and domination by foreigners and by a fierce nation from far away that besieges their cities and drives them to eat their own children. Verses 58-68 close by warning of further plagues, the diseases of Egypt, a people reduced to few in number, scattering among all peoples where they serve other gods, constant fear, and a return to Egypt in ships to be offered as slaves with no buyer.

l: the LORD your God, Deuteronomy, Chapter 28
s: The LORD is the one who will set the Israelites high above all nations and command blessing on them if they obey, and who will send curses, plagues, defeat, and scattering if they do not. He is described as having rejoiced in doing them good, and he will likewise rejoice in destroying them if they disobey. His name is called glorious and fearful.

The Israelites are told that obeying the LORD's voice and commandments brings them blessing, prosperity, and a position as head and not tail. Disobedience is said to bring curses, defeat, disease, siege, exile, and slavery, until they are left few in number despite having been as many as the stars. They are also charged with not having served the LORD with joy in the midst of abundance.

The blessings come upon and overtake those who listen to the LORD, covering city and field, offspring, ground, livestock, basket and kneading trough, and coming in and going out. They include victory over enemies, abundant prosperity, rain in season, and lending to many nations without borrowing. They are conditioned on keeping the commandments and not turning to other gods.

The curses are the reverse of the blessings and are set out at far greater length, running from verse 15 to the end of the chapter. They include confusion, pestilence, disease, drought, defeat, loss of wives, houses, crops, and children, foreign domination, siege cannibalism, and exile. They are said to pursue and overtake the people until they are destroyed, and to serve as a sign and wonder to their offspring forever.

l: commandments, statutes, and ordinances, Deuteronomy, Chapter 28
s: The commandments, along with the statutes and the words of the law written in the book, are what the people must listen to, observe, and do, without turning right or left to other gods. Keeping them leads to blessing, and failing to keep them leads to the curses. Fearing the LORD's name is the stated aim of observing them.

The LORD will bring a nation from the end of the earth against the Israelites, swift as an eagle flies, whose language they will not understand. It is described as fierce in expression and showing no respect for old or young. It will consume their livestock and crops, besiege all their gates until their fortified walls fall, and leave them no grain, wine, or oil.

The boils of Egypt and all the diseases of Egypt, which the Israelites feared, are named among the afflictions the LORD will bring on them. The chapter ends with the LORD bringing them back to Egypt in ships, by a way he said they would never see again. There they will offer themselves as male and female slaves, and nobody will buy them.

The land is the one the LORD swore to the fathers to give, where he will bless the people in their barns and work if they obey. If they disobey, the land turns to bronze sky and iron earth, its rain becomes dust, and its produce is eaten by locusts and worms. The people will be plucked from the land they are going in to possess.

l: exile and scattering among nations, Deuteronomy, Chapter 28
s: The LORD will scatter the Israelites among all peoples from one end of the earth to the other, and bring them and their king to a nation they have not known. There they will serve gods of wood and stone, become an astonishment, proverb, and byword, and find no rest. They will have trembling hearts, failing eyes, and constant fear for their lives.

Moses gathers all Israel in the land of Moab to enter a covenant with the LORD in addition to the one made at Horeb. He recalls the LORD's acts in Egypt, the forty years in the wilderness in which clothes and sandals did not wear out, and the defeat of Sihon and Og, whose land was given to the Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of the Manassites. He stresses that the covenant and oath bind everyone present, from leaders to the foreigner who draws water, and also those not present, and he warns against any man, woman, family, or tribe turning to the gods of the nations. Anyone who hears the curse yet assures himself of peace will not be pardoned, and the LORD will blot out his name. Moses describes how future generations and nations will see the land made sulfur, salt, and burning like Sodom and Gomorrah, and will conclude that Israel abandoned the covenant and was uprooted; he ends by saying secret things belong to the LORD, while revealed things belong to Israel so they may do the law.

l: the LORD your God, Deuteronomy, Chapter 29
s: The LORD commanded Moses to make a covenant in Moab beyond the Horeb covenant, and he is recalled as having led Israel forty years in the wilderness and given them the lands of Sihon and Og. He is said not to have yet given Israel a heart to know, eyes to see, and ears to hear. He will refuse to pardon the one who turns to other gods, blot out his name, and, in the picture of the future, uproot the people in anger and overthrow the land as with Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim.

Moses calls all Israel together and recounts what they saw in Egypt, the wilderness years, and the defeat of Sihon and Og. He explains the terms of the covenant and oath, warns against idolatry and the root of bitter poison, and foretells how future generations and nations will interpret the land's devastation. He closes by stating that the secret things belong to the LORD and the revealed things to Israel.

Israel, including heads, tribes, elders, officers, men, little ones, wives, and foreigners, stands before the LORD to enter his covenant and oath, by which he establishes them as his people. They are reminded of Egypt, the wilderness, and victories over Sihon and Og, and are told they have not yet been given a heart to know. They are warned that abandoning the covenant for other gods would bring the curses and expulsion from their land.

This covenant is made in the land of Moab in addition to the one made at Horeb, and is sworn by the LORD to establish Israel as his people as he swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. It binds those present and those not present. Its words are to be kept so Israel may prosper, and abandoning it is the stated reason later nations will give for the land's ruin.

l: curses of the covenant, Deuteronomy, Chapter 29
s: The curses are written in this book of the law and are said to fall on anyone who hears them yet blesses himself in his heart while walking in stubbornness. They would set that person apart for evil out of all the tribes and blot out his name. They are also the cause of the LORD's anger burning against the land and the uprooting of the people.

Any man, woman, family, or tribe whose heart turns to serve the gods of the nations is described as a root producing bitter poison. If he hears the curse and assures himself of peace despite his stubborn heart, the LORD will not pardon him, his anger and jealousy will smoke against him, and his name will be blotted out from under the sky.

The land is foretold as a place of plagues and sicknesses, all sulfur, salt, and burning, unsown, unproductive, and without grass, like Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim.
