Future generations, foreigners, and nations will ask why the LORD did this and will be told it was because the people abandoned the covenant and served other gods, so the LORD uprooted them from it.

In Chapter 30, the speaker promises that after the Israelites experience the blessing and the curse and take them to heart among the nations where the LORD has driven them, they can return to the LORD with all their heart and soul. The LORD will then release them from captivity, gather them from every distant place, bring them back to the land of their fathers, circumcise their hearts, and prosper them, while putting the curses on their enemies. The speaker says the commandment is not too hard or too distant, not in heaven or beyond the sea, but very near, in their mouth and heart. He sets before them life and prosperity against death and evil, and calls heaven and earth as witnesses. He urges them to choose life by loving the LORD, obeying his voice, and clinging to him, so that they may dwell in the land sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

l: the LORD your God, Deuteronomy, Chapter 30
s: The LORD your God is said to release the exiles from captivity, have compassion on them, and gather them from all the peoples where he scattered them, even from the uttermost parts of the heavens. He will bring them into the land, do them good, circumcise their hearts so they love him, put the curses on their enemies, and again rejoice over them as he did over their fathers. He is described as the Israelites' life and the length of their days, and the one who swore the land to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

The Israelites are told that after the blessing and curse come on them and they are driven among the nations, they will call these to mind, return to the LORD, and obey his voice with all their heart and soul. They are promised restoration and prosperity if they obey. They are given a choice between life and death, and told that turning away to worship other gods will cause them to perish and not prolong their days in the land.

The land is the place the LORD will bring the scattered Israelites back to, where they will possess it as their fathers did and increase in number. It lies across the Jordan, and remaining in it for long depends on loving and obeying the LORD. It is the land the LORD swore to give to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

The blessing and the curse are set before the Israelites, who are expected to call them to mind among the nations after they have come upon them. The LORD will put all the curses on the Israelites' enemies and on those who hate and persecuted them. In the closing appeal, the blessing and the curse are paired with life and death as the choice the Israelites face.

l: commandments, statutes, and ordinances, Deuteronomy, Chapter 30
s: The commandment is what the speaker commands today, and it is written in this book of the law along with the LORD's statutes. It is declared not too hard or too distant, neither in heaven nor beyond the sea, but very near, in the people's mouth and heart so that they may do it. It centers on loving the LORD, walking in his ways, and keeping his commandments, statutes, and ordinances.

l: life and death choice, Deuteronomy, Chapter 30
s: The speaker sets before the Israelites life and prosperity on one side and death and evil on the other, and calls heaven and earth as witnesses. Loving and obeying the LORD leads to life, multiplication, and blessing in the land, while turning away to other gods means certain perishing. The Israelites are urged to choose life, for themselves and their descendants, by loving the LORD, obeying his voice, and clinging to him.

l: exile and scattering among nations, Deuteronomy, Chapter 30
s: The chapter foresees the Israelites driven by the LORD among all the nations after the blessing and curse come on them. If they call these to mind, return, and obey with all their heart and soul, the LORD will release them from captivity, gather them from every place of scattering, and bring them back to the land. Restoration includes the circumcision of their hearts, increased numbers, prosperity, and the LORD's renewed rejoicing over them.

Moses, aged 120, tells all Israel he can no longer lead and that the LORD will go before them and give them victory, with Joshua as their leader. He encourages Joshua publicly, writes down the law, gives it to the priests and elders, and orders it read to all Israel every seven years at the feast of booths. The LORD summons Moses and Joshua to the Tent of Meeting, commissions Joshua, and predicts that Israel will turn to other gods and suffer for it. He instructs Moses to write a song as a witness against Israel, and Moses writes and teaches it. Moses then has the Levites place the law book beside the ark as a witness against Israel's rebellion, and he speaks the song to the whole assembly.

Moses, aged 120, tells Israel he cannot go over the Jordan, encourages the people and Joshua, writes the law, and commands its public reading every seven years. He is told by the LORD that he will die and that Israel will rebel, writes and teaches the song, has the Levites place the law book by the ark, and speaks the song to the whole assembly.

l: the LORD your God, Deuteronomy, Chapter 31
s: The LORD is said to go before Israel, destroy the nations as he did to Sihon and Og, and never fail or forsake them. He commissions Joshua at the Tent of Meeting in a pillar of cloud, foretells that Israel will forsake him and that he will hide his face, and commands Moses to write the song as a witness.

Joshua is named as the one who will go over before Israel, and Moses charges him before all Israel to be strong and courageous. The LORD commissions him at the Tent of Meeting, and he is told he will bring Israel into the land the LORD swore to give.

Israel is told that the LORD will give them the land and that they must obey the law and hear it read every seven years, including women, children and foreigners. The LORD predicts they will prosper, turn to other gods, break the covenant, and suffer evils, and Moses says he knows their rebellion and stiff neck. They are taught the song.

The land is described as sworn by the LORD to Israel's fathers and flowing with milk and honey, and Israel will cross the Jordan to possess it. The LORD predicts that once Israel has eaten and grown fat there, they will turn to other gods.

l: commandments, statutes, and ordinances, Deuteronomy, Chapter 31
s: Moses writes the law, gives it to the priests and elders, and commands that it be read to all Israel every seven years at the feast of booths. After he finishes writing it in a book, the Levites are told to put it beside the ark as a witness against Israel.

The LORD tells Moses to write the song and teach it to Israel as a witness against them, since it will not be forgotten by their descendants. Moses writes it the same day, teaches it to the people, and speaks its words to the whole assembly.

The LORD foretells that Israel will play the prostitute after the strange gods of the land, serving them, despising him, and breaking his covenant. This turning to other gods is given as the cause of the LORD hiding his face and of the evils that will come on Israel.

Chapter 32 presents the Song of Moses, in which Moses calls heaven and earth to hear him proclaim the LORD as the faithful, just Rock. The song recounts how the LORD found Jacob in the wilderness, cared for him, and gave him rich provision, but Jeshurun grew fat, abandoned God, and sacrificed to demons and new gods. The LORD responds with anger, announcing famine, plague, beasts, and the sword, yet restrains himself from erasing Israel lest the enemies boast. He declares that vengeance is his, that there is no god beside him, and that he will avenge his servants and atone for his land and people. Moses and Joshua son of Nun recite the song to all Israel, Moses urges them to obey the law as their life, and the LORD tells Moses to go up Mount Nebo, view Canaan, and die there because of his trespass at Meribah of Kadesh.

l: the LORD your God, Deuteronomy, Chapter 32
s: The LORD is praised as the Rock whose work is perfect and whose ways are just, who found Israel in the wilderness, cared for him like an eagle with her young, and provided abundantly. Angered by Israel's idolatry, he vows to hide his face and send calamity, but holds back from destroying them fully so the enemy cannot claim credit. He declares that there is no god beside him, that he kills and makes alive, wounds and heals, and that he will judge his people, show compassion to his servants, and take vengeance on his adversaries.

Israel, called Jacob and Jeshurun, is described as the LORD's portion, found in the wilderness and richly provided for. It grew fat, abandoned the Rock who made it, and is called a perverse and crooked generation, void of counsel. It is threatened with severe judgment but is promised that the LORD will have compassion on his servants and atone for his land and people.

Moses speaks the song to the people, with Joshua son of Nun, and finishes reciting all its words to all Israel. He charges them to set their hearts on the words of the law and teach them to their children, because they are their life. The LORD then tells him to go up Mount Nebo, see Canaan, and die there, because he trespassed at Meribah of Kadesh and did not uphold the LORD's holiness.

Mount Nebo, in the Abarim range in the land of Moab across from Jericho, is the place the LORD tells Moses to climb. From there Moses will see the land of Canaan from a distance. He is to die on that mountain and be gathered to his people, as Aaron was on Mount Hor.

Canaan is the land the LORD is giving to the children of Israel as a possession. Moses is told he may see it from Mount Nebo but will not enter it. Israel is told that obeying the law will prolong their days in the land across the Jordan.

The strange gods are described as demons and not God, new gods that arose recently, unknown to Israel and not dreaded by their fathers. Their worship provoked the LORD to jealousy and anger. The LORD mocks them, asking where these gods are and challenging them to rise up and protect Israel, since the one who ate their sacrifices cannot save them.

The song is a poem beginning with a call to heaven and earth to hear. It praises the LORD as the faithful Rock, recounts his care for Israel, accuses Israel of apostasy, announces judgment and later vengeance on adversaries, and ends with the nations invited to rejoice. Moses and Joshua recite it to the people, and Moses tells them to take all its words to heart.

l: divine judgment and vengeance, Deuteronomy, Chapter 32
s: The LORD announces judgment on Israel through fire, hunger, burning heat, wild beasts, venom, and the sword, which will bring terror to young and old alike. He restrains total destruction so the enemy cannot boast, then declares that vengeance and recompense are his and that he will repay his adversaries with his sword. The song closes with the promise that he will avenge his servants' blood and make atonement for his land and people.

Israel is accused of dealing corruptly, forgetting the Rock who bore them, and rejecting the God of their salvation after growing prosperous. They provoked the LORD to jealousy with strange gods, abominations, and sacrifices to demons. This apostasy leads the LORD to hide his face and bring calamity, and to provoke Israel in turn with a foolish nation that is not a people.

Chapter 33 presents the blessing with which Moses, the man of God, blessed the children of Israel before his death. It opens by describing the LORD coming from Sinai, Seir, and Mount Paran with a fiery law, and notes that Moses commanded a law as an inheritance for Jacob's assembly. Moses then blesses the tribes in turn, including Reuben, Judah, Levi, Benjamin, Joseph, Zebulun, Issachar, Gad, Dan, Naphtali, and Asher, each with a distinct word about protection, land, strength, or service. The chapter closes by praising God, who rides the heavens and is an eternal dwelling place with everlasting arms, and by declaring Israel happy as a people saved by the LORD whose enemies will submit to them.

Moses, called the man of God, pronounces a blessing on the children of Israel before his death. He is said to have commanded a law as an inheritance for the assembly of Jacob, and he speaks the blessings of each tribe in turn.

l: the LORD your God, Deuteronomy, Chapter 33
s: The LORD is described as coming from Sinai, rising from Seir, and shining from Mount Paran with ten thousands of holy ones and a fiery law at his right hand. He loves the people, blesses Joseph's land, and is praised as the eternal God, a dwelling place with everlasting arms who thrust out the enemy before Israel. He is also the one who saves Israel as a shield and sword.

Israel is the people blessed by Moses, gathered with all its tribes when the LORD was king in Jeshurun. The chapter ends by declaring Israel happy, a people saved by the LORD who dwells in safety in a land of grain and new wine, whose enemies will submit and whose high places it will tread on.

Moses says the Thummim and Urim are with Levi, the LORD's godly one, who was proved at Massah and contended with at the waters of Meribah. Levi did not acknowledge his father, mother, brothers, or children because they observed the LORD's word and covenant. Levi will teach Jacob the ordinances and Israel the law, offer incense and whole burnt offerings, and Moses asks the LORD to bless his skills and strike down those who rise against him.

Moses says Joseph's land is blessed by the LORD with the precious things of the heavens, dew, the deep, the fruits of the sun and moon, the ancient mountains, and the earth's fullness. The blessing is to come on the head of Joseph, who was separated from his brothers. His majesty is compared to the firstborn of a herd with wild ox horns that will push the peoples to the earth's ends, namely the ten thousands of Ephraim and the thousands of Manasseh.

The blessing of Moses is the whole chapter, a series of words spoken to the tribes of Israel before Moses died. It begins with praise of the LORD's coming and the law, then addresses each tribe individually, and ends with praise of God and of Israel as a people saved by the LORD.

Moses goes up from the plains of Moab to Mount Nebo, to the top of Pisgah opposite Jericho, where the LORD shows him the whole land from Gilead to Dan, Naphtali, Ephraim, Manasseh, Judah, the Western Sea, the south, and the plain of Jericho to Zoar. The LORD tells him this is the land sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, but that Moses will see it and not cross over. Moses dies there in Moab at age 120, with undimmed eyes and undiminished strength, and is buried in a valley opposite Beth Peor, his tomb unknown to this day. The children of Israel mourn him for thirty days. Joshua the son of Nun, filled with the spirit of wisdom because Moses laid hands on him, is obeyed by Israel, and the chapter ends by saying no prophet since has equaled Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face.

Moses climbs Mount Nebo to the top of Pisgah, is shown the whole land by the LORD, and is told he will not go over into it. He dies in the land of Moab at age 120, with his eye not dim and his strength not gone, and is remembered as the unmatched prophet whom the LORD knew face to face, in signs, wonders, and mighty deeds done before Pharaoh and all Israel.

l: the LORD your God, Deuteronomy, Chapter 34
s: The LORD shows Moses all the land from Gilead to Dan, Naphtali, Ephraim, Manasseh, Judah, the south, and the plain of Jericho, and recalls his oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob to give it to their offspring. He tells Moses he will see it but not enter, and Moses dies according to the LORD's word. The LORD is said to have known Moses face to face and sent him to do signs and wonders in Egypt.
Joshua the son of Nun is described as full of the spirit of wisdom because Moses had laid his hands on him. The children of Israel listen to him and do as the LORD commanded Moses.
The children of Israel weep for Moses in the plains of Moab for thirty days, until the days of mourning end. They then listen to Joshua and do as the LORD commanded Moses.
Mount Nebo is where Moses goes up from the plains of Moab, to the top of Pisgah opposite Jericho. From there the LORD shows him the whole land he will not enter.
The plains of Moab are the place from which Moses departs to ascend Mount Nebo. The children of Israel weep for him there for thirty days.

The land is shown to Moses from Pisgah, extending from Gilead to Dan, Naphtali, Ephraim, Manasseh, Judah to the Western Sea, the south, and the plain of Jericho to Zoar. The LORD identifies it as the land sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob for their offspring, but Moses will not cross into it.

l: Moses' death and burial, Deuteronomy, Chapter 34
s: Moses dies in the land of Moab according to the LORD's word, at one hundred twenty years old. He is buried in a valley opposite Beth Peor, but no one knows where his tomb is to this day.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah / Chapter 1
s: Isaiah the son of Amoz records his vision concerning Judah and Jerusalem during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. The LORD accuses Israel of rebelling against the children he raised, calls the nation sinful and wounded, and describes its land as desolate and its cities burned, with only a small remnant spared from being like Sodom and Gomorrah. The LORD rejects the people's sacrifices, feasts, and prayers because their hands are full of blood, and commands them to cease evil, seek justice, and defend the fatherless and widow. He offers to make their scarlet sins white as snow if they are willing and obedient, but threatens the sword if they refuse. The chapter laments that the faithful city has become a prostitute with rebellious princes, and promises that the LORD will purge her dross, restore her judges, and redeem Zion with justice while the transgressors are consumed.
